title: Two in the desert (Bava Metzia 62a)
hook: one flask, two travelers; Rabbi Akiva teaches that your own life comes first

segments.voice: Yesterday Beruriah gave back what was entrusted. Your line was they were on loan. Did you treat something precious with care? Day two hundred eighty-five.

Every flight, the same speech. In case of a loss of cabin pressure, put on your own mask before helping others. To some ears it sounds almost selfish. Shouldn't you help the child first? Then the logic lands: if you pass out, you can't help anyone. The Talmud has a much older, much harder version of that same question. Two people are walking through the desert. Only one of them has water. And there isn't enough for two. Today, two sages disagree about what to do.
screen: `PUT ON YOUR OWN MASK FIRST.` → `TWO IN THE DESERT.` → `WATER ENOUGH FOR ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the case, in tractate Bava Metzia. Two people are traveling, and one has a flask of water. If both drink, both will die. If one drinks, he'll reach the next town alive. What should he do? A sage named Ben Petura taught: better that both drink and both die, than that one watch the other die. Share it, whatever happens. It's a beautiful, brave answer. Then Rabbi Akiva came and taught from a verse in Leviticus: "that thy brother may live with thee." With thee, Akiva said. Your brother lives with you, alongside you. So your own life comes first. The one with the flask may drink. The Talmud frames it this way: Ben Petura taught, until Rabbi Akiva came and taught otherwise. Now, this isn't a license for selfishness. Look where the verse comes from: it's about lending to someone in need without charging interest, about keeping your brother alive. And look at the case: it's an extreme one, where sharing means certain death for both. Akiva isn't saying ignore other people. He's saying you're a person too. Your life counts in the math. The airline card says something close, in a calmer voice: you can't care for anyone if you've collapsed. Akiva's word is with: your life comes first, and your brother's lives alongside it.
screen: `ONE FLASK, TWO TRAVELERS.` · `BEN PETURA: BOTH DRINK.` · `AKIVA: THAT HE MAY LIVE WITH THEE.` · `NOT SELFISH: YOU COUNT TOO.` · then, large: `YOUR LIFE COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check your own flask. Settle, and breathe. Where are you running low right now? Sleep, food, quiet, time with friends, a doctor's appointment you keep putting off. Notice who depends on you. Now notice that they depend on you being alive and well. Pick one small thing that would refill your flask today. Water. A walk. Going to bed on time. Picture doing it, not as a treat, but as part of caring for them. The bell holds the time.
Rabbi Akiva, who taught that with one flask between two travelers in the desert, your life comes first, and your brother lives with you.
Your line: your life comes first. Today, do one thing that refills your own flask, so you have something to give. Day two hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Jewish ethics takes care of one's own health seriously, and Akiva's ruling, chayekha kodmin, your life comes first, is discussed in Jewish writing on triage and self-sacrifice.

fork.setup: two of you in the desert. you have the only flask. if you share, both die. if you drink, you reach town. what does Rabbi Akiva say?
options: pour it out so no one has an unfair advantage.
fork.reveal: Akiva read that thy brother may live with thee: your life comes first. Ben Petura had said both should drink.

trapdoor: what you thought: every man for himself.
what it means: in a real either-or, your life counts too, and then your brother's with it.
what a scholar hears: Akiva reads the word with thee in Leviticus 25:36, a verse about interest-free loans, and the Talmud says Ben Petura taught until Akiva came.

notes: Bava Metzia 62a paraphrased. 'Better that both drink and die than that one see his fellow's death' is Ben Petura's view.
'Most later Jewish law follows Rabbi Akiva': standard, but decisors discuss scope; please confirm wording.
The airline analogy is modern and framed as an analogy only.
